strengths: The paper addresses a clear and timely problem: the quadratic self-attention bottleneck in video diffusion transformers. The proposed data-free post-training formulation is practical and well-motivated, removing the need for curated training data by sampling (x_t, u_t) pairs along the original model's own sampling trajectory.

The 'selective transfer' mechanism is a sensible and well-supported contribution. The empirical observation in Fig. 2 (shallow layers are far easier to linearize than early/certain layers) is an interesting finding, and casting layer replacement as a binary classification with a learnable score, a constraint loss, and a rounding-friendly regularizer (Eq. 9-10) is a clean solution. The ablation (Tab. 3) confirms it substantially outperforms manual and heuristic layer selection.

The anytime distribution matching (ADM) objective is well-reasoned: it correctly identifies that (i) matching only p_0 discards intermediate-timestep distributions and (ii) requiring an auxiliary multi-step score model (as in DMD-style distillation) is expensive. The insight that a linearized flow model can estimate its own score (Eq. 13) is elegant and avoids the auxiliary model entirely, yielding a claimed ~4.4x training-time reduction and better quality than L_DMD variants (Tab. 4, Fig. 8).

The empirical evaluation is thorough for the settings studied: VBench and VBench-2.0 comparisons against several sparse-attention baselines (SVG, SVG2, XAttn, DFA), VBench-2.0 total score exceeding SVG2 (56.74 vs 55.81), ablations over target count, lambda, and regularizers, plus end-to-end latency scaling across frame counts (81-521 frames) showing growing advantage (1.52-2.00x at 521 frames).

The 4-step distilled result (15.92x end-to-end speedup with ~1% VBench drop) is a strong practical outcome and, to the authors' credit, they show Ours+DMD2 slightly degrades on some metrics rather than hiding it. The paper is generally clearly written with honest framing of trade-offs (e.g., speedup/quality trade-off in Tab. 2).
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is limited to a single model: all main results are on Wan 1.3B at 832x480, 16 FPS, 5s videos. There is no evidence the framework transfers to other video DMs (e.g., CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo, larger Wan variants) or other architectures, which weakens the generality of the 'first data-free post-training framework' claim. The 30-layer structure analyzed is specific to Wan 1.3B.

The headline speedup of the multi-step model is modest: 1.43x average latency reduction at 81 frames, with the larger 1.52-2.00x gains only appearing at 500+ frames. The impressive 15.92x figure relies on 4-step DMD2 distillation, which is an orthogonal technique; conflating these in the abstract may overstate the contribution of linearization itself. Additionally, no specialized kernel is implemented for the linear-attention path, so reported latency may not reflect the achievable optimum.

The claim of 'lossless' or 'preserving performance' is slightly stronger than the evidence: Tab. 1 shows small but consistent drops versus FlashAttention2 (e.g., Aesthetic Quality 57.41 vs 59.49 for Ours+DMD2, Overall Consistency 25.94 vs 26.18), and quality degrades non-trivially once target >18 layers (Tab. 2: Overall Consistency drops from 26.52 at target=16 to 23.30 at target=20).

Several theoretical steps rely on assumptions that are asserted rather than fully validated in the main text: the ADM gradient form (Eq. 12-13) depends on the linearized model being a valid flow model throughout training and on self-score estimation being accurate; the derivation is deferred to the appendix and no direct diagnostic (e.g., measured score error) is provided in the main paper.

Some baselines are excluded with justification that may not fully satisfy readers: methods requiring substantially more training resources [66] and methods supporting only specific video shapes [25] are omitted, and comparisons to actual pretrained linear-attention video models (e.g., SANA-Video) are discussed only as related work rather than benchmarked. A direct comparison with SLA [63] (intra-layer mixed attention post-training, the closest concurrent approach) would strengthen the contribution claims.

Reproducibility details are partially deferred to the appendix (grid-search details, alpha annealing schedule, DMD2 fine-tuning configuration), and there is no explicit statement of code/model release; the 8 H100 GPU x 3K-step training cost, while reasonable, is nontrivial for reproduction.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: the quadratic cost of self-attention in video diffusion transformers. The proposed solution—post-training replacement of a target number of softmax attention layers with linear attention—is well motivated, and the claim of being the first data-free post-training linearization framework for video DMs appears defensible given the related work discussion (e.g., contrast with SLA's intra-layer mixed attention).

The two technical components are reasonable and clearly described. Selective transfer casts layer selection as a binary classification problem with a learnable score r, a constraint loss on the target count (Eq. 9), and a quantization-inspired regularization (Eq. 10) to drive scores toward 0/1; this is a sensible, training-based alternative to manual or heuristic layer choice, and the ablation (Table 3) shows large gains over a heuristic baseline (26.52 vs. 18.94 Overall Consistency).

The anytime distribution matching (ADM) objective is the more interesting contribution. The observation that few-step distribution matching only aligns p_0 and requires an auxiliary multi-step teacher to estimate the score is well argued, and the rectified-flow identity (Eq. 13) letting the model estimate its own score is elegant. Table 4 and Fig. 8 support the claims: ADM substantially outperforms the naive L_mse and L_DMD objectives while requiring ~4.4x less training time than a learned score approximator.

The empirical study of layer replaceability (Fig. 2)—shallow layers linearize more easily, and errors in early layers (e.g., layer 1) are not recoverable by further fine-tuning—is a useful empirical finding for anyone attempting similar linearization.

Ablations are fairly thorough: target count (Table 2), selective transfer strategy and lambda (Table 3), the regularization term, and the training objective (Table 4), plus efficiency measurements at multiple resolutions and frame counts (Fig. 6, 7).
weaknesses: Generality is unproven: all main experiments use a single model (Wan 1.3B) at a single resolution (832x480, 5s, 16fps). The claims about which layers are replaceable and the effectiveness of ADM may be model-specific; no second backbone (e.g., HunyuanVideo, CogVideoX) is evaluated. For a paper whose central claim is a general post-training framework, this is a significant limitation.

The headline efficiency gain is modest. Replacing 16/30 attention layers yields ~1.43x average end-to-end speedup (1.25-2.00x range, Fig. 6), and the paper itself notes no custom kernel is used. The 15.92x figure comes from combining with 4-step DMD2 distillation, which is largely attributable to step reduction rather than linear attention. The abstract's framing risks overstating the contribution of linearization per se.

Quality improvements over baselines are small and the comparison fairness is questionable. In Table 1, differences between Ours (26.52 Overall Consistency) and sparse baselines are within noise margins; notably, the SVG2 row appears to report 26.87 on Overall Consistency—higher than Ours—while the text claims LINVIDEO 'consistently far outperforms all sparse-attention baselines.' This inconsistency between the table and the narrative needs clarification. Furthermore, baselines were restricted (RMSNorm kernels excluded, methods requiring more training or specific shapes excluded), and sparse methods were not given the same fine-tuning budget as LinVideo's 2K+3K training steps.

Potential selective reporting in evaluation: the authors 'select 8 dimensions in VBench' without full justification for the selection, and the VBench-2.0 comparison (Fig. 4) is radar-chart only, making exact per-dimension differences hard to verify; the total-score advantage over SVG2 (56.74 vs. 55.81) is again small.

The data-free protocol depends on 50K (x_t, u_t) pairs collected along the sampling trajectory of the original model; the paper gives little detail on prompt sourcing for these pairs, so distributional coverage and possible quality ceilings of this data-free strategy are unclear. Some important details (grid search for the heuristic baseline, alpha annealing schedule, appendix derivations) are deferred to an appendix not provided here.

Novelty is incremental in parts: the finding that shallow layers are easier to replace is intuitive, and the components (Hedgehog kernel, STE-based scoring, DMD2 distillation) are largely assembled from prior work; the main novelty lies in the ADM objective and the combination.

No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned, which is a concern given that results depend on many implementation choices (target selection, lambda, annealing, training schedules on 8 H100 GPUs).

strengths: The problem is well motivated and timely: self-attention in video DMs scales quadratically with sequence length and is a genuine deployment bottleneck, and the paper targets an under-explored setting—data-free post-training linearization of a pre-trained video DM—rather than costly pretraining from scratch.

The two proposed techniques are reasonable and well-designed: (i) 'selective transfer' casts layer selection as a learnable binary classification with a constraint loss (Eq. 9) and a regularization term (Eq. 10) to avoid the observed r≈0.5 fluctuation; (ii) ADM (Sec. 4.2) is a clever adaptation of distribution matching that aligns distributions across all timesteps along the sampling trajectory, avoiding both temporal artifacts of the naive L_mse and the extra multi-step score model required by few-step DM objectives.

Empirical support is substantial: VBench (Tab. 1) shows LinVideo outperforming multiple strong sparse-attention baselines (SVG, SVG2, XAttn, DFA) and even dense FlashAttention2 on Overall Consistency (26.52 vs 26.18); VBench-2.0 results (Fig. 4) with augmented prompts further support quality; qualitative results are included.

Ablations are thorough and directly validate each design choice: target value sweep (Tab. 2), selective transfer vs. manual vs. heuristic selection (Tab. 3), regularization effect (Fig. 3), and objective comparisons showing L_ADM beats L_mse and L_DMD by large margins (21.46 and 16.96 overall consistency vs 26.52) while cutting training cost by ~4.4× vs. a DMD-style variant (Fig. 8).

The efficiency analysis is honest: end-to-end latency is measured on real hardware across step counts and frame counts (Fig. 6, 7), showing 1.25–2.00× speedup scaling with sequence length and a 15.92× end-to-end speedup when combined with 4-step DMD2 distillation, with <1% and <3% quality drops respectively.

The paper is clearly written, positions itself carefully against concurrent work (SLA, SANA-Video, LinGen), and addresses a practically important question (can linear attention be adopted post-training without pretraining?) with a positive answer supported by evidence.
weaknesses: Generalization is unverified: all experiments use a single model (Wan 1.3B) at a single resolution. It is unclear whether the shallow-layer replaceability finding (Fig. 2), the ADM objective, and the layer-selection mechanism transfer to larger DiTs, different architectures (e.g., cross-attention-heavy designs), or image DMs. A second backbone would substantially strengthen the claims.

The acceleration is modest in the default setting: target=16 (16/30 layers linearized) yields only ~1.43× average speedup, and even the extreme setting is 2.00× at 531 frames. Half the attention layers remain quadratic, so the practical O(n) promise is only partially realized; the authors themselves note that integrating sparse attention is left as future work. Compared to sparse-attention methods that achieve larger speedups at higher resolutions, the efficiency argument is not dominant—quality retention is the main selling point.

Evaluation relies exclusively on VBench/VBench-2.0 automated metrics; no human evaluation is provided, and the visual comparisons (Fig. 5) are limited. Since linear-attention substitution can introduce subtle spatiotemporal artifacts, human studies would better substantiate the 'preserves quality' claim.

Novelty is somewhat incremental at the component level: the linear kernel is taken directly from Hedgehog (Eq. 6), the layer-selection mechanism is a straightforward application of learnable gates with STE (common in NAS/quantization), and the ADM objective builds on Ma et al.'s score self-estimation property (Eq. 13). The contribution is more in the combination and the video-linearization insight than in fundamentally new machinery.

Key details supporting the main claims are deferred to the appendix (derivation of Eq. 13, heuristic selection details, annealing schedule for α, temporal artifacts of L_mse), so the main text is not fully self-contained; reproducibility depends on those appendices, and no code release is mentioned.

The layer-replaceability analysis (Fig. 2) is based on only five adjacent-layer configurations on one model; the broader claim that shallow layers are inherently easier to linearize would benefit from a wider empirical study.

Some comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: baselines like SVG/XAttn use larger base models and different acceleration mechanisms, and the paper excludes methods requiring more training or specific sparse shapes, which—while reasonably justified—limits the completeness of the competitive landscape.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: the quadratic cost of self-attention in video diffusion transformers. The proposed post-training, data-free linearization framework is, to my knowledge, novel — prior linear-attention video models (Matten, LinGen, SANA-Video) require costly pretraining, and the concurrent SLA work focuses on intra-layer rather than inter-layer mixed attention, so the distinction and positioning are clearly articulated.

Selective transfer is a clean and sensible formulation: casting per-layer replacement as a binary classification with a learnable score r, plus constraint (Eq. 9) and regularization (Eq. 10) losses, elegantly automates layer selection. The empirical motivation (Fig. 2 showing large performance disparity across replaced layers) is convincing, and the ablation (Tab. 3) shows the learned selection clearly outperforms manual and heuristic alternatives.

The anytime distribution matching (ADM) objective is well-grounded: the analysis of why naive matching (temporal artifacts) and few-step distribution matching (matches only p0, requires a costly auxiliary score model) fail in this setting is insightful, and matching distributions at arbitrary timesteps along the trajectory (Eq. 11-13, with a derived score-difference form leveraging the model itself) is a technically sound contribution that also cuts training cost by ~4.4x versus DMD2-style alternatives (Fig. 6, Tab. 4).

Experiments are reasonably thorough: two model scales (Wan 1.3B and 14B), evaluation on both VBench and VBench-2.0 across many dimensions, comparison against four sparse-attention baselines with end-to-end latency on the same hardware, ablations over target, lambda, and the annealing range of alpha, plus an appendix covering implementation details, score derivation, qualitative failure cases of the naive objective, and a two-stage pipeline with 4-step DMD2 distillation yielding 15.9-20.9x speedup with minor quality loss.

The paper is generally well written and well organized, with honest discussion of limitations (e.g., lack of specialized linear-attention kernels, ~1% quality drop with DMD2, orthogonality to sparse-attention methods).
weaknesses: The end-to-end speedup of the main model is modest (1.43-1.71x). Because the method retains dense quadratic attention in un-replaced layers and uses no optimized linear-attention kernel, the practical efficiency gain is smaller than what sparsification approaches achieve in some regimes. The authors acknowledge this, but the headline efficiency claim is not dramatic on its own; the value rests mainly on quality preservation at moderate speedup.

Evaluation relies exclusively on automated metrics (VBench/VBench-2.0). No human evaluation or FVD on a real video dataset is provided, so the claim of 'lossless' or quality-preserving acceleration rests entirely on benchmark scores of limited fidelity, some of which (aesthetic quality, imaging quality) are known to be noisy.

Generality of the evaluation is narrow in terms of base models: both models are from the same Wan family with rectified-flow parameterization. The ADM derivation (Eq. 13) exploits the specific (1-t, t) schedule; applicability to other DM parameterizations (e.g., discrete-time, v-prediction) is not demonstrated.

The 'data-free' framing deserves more scrutiny: training still depends on the prompt distribution from OpenVid (50K input/output pairs collected over 81-frame latents). This is data-free in the sense of no real video data, but the method's quality and generalization may hinge on the prompt set, and the paper does not ablate sensitivity to the prompt source or the amount of collected data.

Some important details are deferred or underspecified in the main text: how the mixed-attention layer (Eq. 8) is instantiated at inference (both branches computed during training implies a training-inference mismatch whose cost/behavior is not analyzed), and the target hyper-parameter must be set a priori (16 or 22) — a principled way to choose it is not provided, though the target ablation (Tab. 2) partially mitigates this concern.

Baseline comparability could be questioned: the authors compare only 'fast attention implementations' of competing methods and exclude SLA due to a hardware-specific kernel, which is a reasonable but self-serving exclusion; a broader comparison (e.g., including quantization-combined methods referenced as [24, 63]) would strengthen the case.

Ablations of the selection strategy (Tab. 3) are performed at a single target value on the 1.3B model only; whether selective transfer remains superior at other operating points or at 14B scale is not shown.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: self-attention is a genuine bottleneck for video DMs, and the paper correctly identifies why existing linear-attention approaches (costly pretraining from scratch) and sparsification methods (diminishing returns at moderate sequence lengths) do not solve it.

Technically interesting contributions: (i) 'selective transfer' casts layer replacement as a learnable binary classification with a constraint loss (Eq. 9) and a quantization-inspired regularization (Eq. 10), which is a clean, automated alternative to manual/heuristic layer selection; (ii) 'anytime distribution matching' (ADM) extends distribution matching from only the final sample distribution to any timestep along the sampling trajectory, and cleverly exploits the flow-model property that u_theta can self-estimate the score, removing the need for an expensive auxiliary score model (Eq. 13).

Strong empirical support: results on two model scales (Wan 1.3B and 14B), comparison against multiple sparse-attention baselines (SVG, SVG2, DFA, XAttn), VBench and VBench-2.0 evaluation, and an unusually thorough ablation suite (target count, selection method, lambda, alpha annealing, training objective, training cost in Fig. 6). The ablations directly support each design choice (e.g., ADM beats L_dmd and the s_tilde variant at ~4.4x lower training cost; L_reg prevents r from fluctuating near 0.5).

The two-stage pipeline (linearization then DMD2 distillation) is well justified: the appendix convincingly shows that directly combining few-step distillation with linearization collapses (Table II, Overall 11.06), while the staged approach attains 15.9-20.9x speedup with only ~1% quality drop.

The paper is honest about limitations: it explicitly notes the modest speedup without a specialized kernel, the orthogonality to sparse-attention methods, and exclusion of baselines requiring special hardware/kernels.
Claimed first data-free post-training linearization of video DMs appears plausible given the related work (SLA is concurrent and intra-layer rather than inter-layer).
weaknesses: The headline speedup is modest: 1.43-1.71x end-to-end with dense linear attention, only slightly above SVG (1.31-1.61x). Much of the practical appeal rests on the distilled 4-step variant, which itself borrows heavily from existing DMD2 work.

Quality is not fully 'lossless' as the conclusion claims: Table 1 shows the distilled LinVideo+DMD2 degrades several metrics (e.g., Aesthetic Quality 57.74 vs 65.29 for Wan 1.3B; Overall Consistency 25.94 vs 26.18), and VBench-2.0 totals show a drop for the 14B model (59.62 vs 59.85 for FA2). The Dynamic Degree metric in Table 1 for the 1.3B LinVideo (59.67) exceeding the teacher (58.42) is surprising and not explained.

Evaluation breadth is limited: only 8 dimensions of VBench with unaugmented prompts in the main table, no human evaluation, no FVD, and no evaluation on other backbones beyond Wan. The 'data-free' setup relies on prompts from OpenVid, so it is data-free only in the sense of not needing paired training videos; dependence on the prompt distribution is not analyzed.

Mixed-attention formulation (Eq. 8) with r not exactly 0/1 raises an inference-time concern: layers with intermediate r still compute both quadratic and linear branches, and the authors themselves note that removing a layer with r ~ 0.5 by rounding can cause accuracy drops. The STE-based binarization and rounding robustness deserve more analysis than the <10^-3 claim in the ablation.
Scalability of the approach to larger/more recent models is untested beyond Wan, and no code or kernel implementation is released, which limits reproducibility of the reported latencies.
The claim of 'first' to apply few-step distillation to linear-attention video DMs is a relatively narrow novelty claim resting on a specific combination.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: self-attention's O(n^2) cost is a real bottleneck for video diffusion transformers, and the paper's framing — that full linear-attention replacement requires costly pretraining, so a data-free post-training path is the practical question — is compelling and timely.

The two technical contributions are well designed and clearly explained. 'Selective transfer' elegantly converts layer selection into a learnable binary classification problem with a constraint loss and a quantization-inspired regularizer, addressing the empirically demonstrated observation (Fig. 2) that layer choice matters greatly. 'Anytime distribution matching' is a sensible and well-argued objective: it avoids both the temporal artifacts of direct output matching (evidenced in Appendix E) and the cost/limitations of few-step distribution matching, exploiting the property that the current model can estimate its own score under rectified flow (Eq. 13 with derivation in Appendix D).

Extensive and honest experimentation: evaluation on two model scales (Wan 1.3B and 14B), comparison against multiple sparse-attention baselines (SVG, SVG2, DFA, XAttn) under controlled settings (fast-attention-only implementations), an additional VBench-2.0 evaluation, and thorough ablations covering target count, layer-selection strategy, regularizer, and training objective (Tab. 2–4, Fig. 6). The claim of 1.43–1.71x speedup with near-lossless quality and 15.9–20.9x with 4-step distillation is supported by the reported tables.

The ablations substantiate the design choices rather than merely asserting them — e.g., Manual >> Heuristic selection, and ADM outperforming Lmse, L_DMD, and the auxiliary-score variant while being ~4.4x cheaper to train — which strengthens confidence in the method's internal validity.

The related-work positioning is careful, including honest discussion of the concurrent SLA work and why it is not directly compared, plus an explicitly stated limitation that no specialized linear-attention kernel was used (leaving speedup headroom on the table).
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is limited to a single model family (Wan 1.3B/14B). Generalization of the selective-transfer and ADM recipe to other video DiT architectures (e.g., CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo) is unverified, which limits confidence in the framework's claimed generality.

Evaluation relies entirely on automated VBench/VBench-2.0 metrics over a subset of dimensions; no human evaluation or FVD-style quantitative comparison is provided. Some VBench dimensions are known to be imperfect proxies, and 'near-lossless' quality claims would be more convincing with human assessment.

The 'data-free' claim deserves scrutiny: the method collects 50K input/output pairs from the original model over the full sampling trajectory (81 frames per sample), which is itself a substantial data-collection and inference cost. It is data-free with respect to external curated datasets, but not free of significant teacher-generated data generation.

The absolute speedup (1.43–1.71x) is modest compared to what specialized kernels might achieve, and the comparison to SLA (potentially a stronger competitor) is excluded due to hardware constraints (RTX 5090-only kernel). The end-to-end latency comparison also depends on implementation details (batch size 1, single H100) that may not reflect all deployment regimes.

The method still retains a target number of quadratic attention layers (16 of 40 for 1.3B), so it is a mixed-attention solution whose speedup saturates; the interplay with orthogonal sparsification is left to future work rather than demonstrated.

Several key details (heuristic search procedure, alpha annealing behavior, full training configs) are deferred to the appendix; reproducibility would benefit from the promised code release, which is not explicitly stated in the manuscript.
